RETRIEVE · EXPLAIN · CHECK · RETRY

Student revision

Find a weak topic, explain it without notes, check your reasoning and try a changed case later.

2026 foundation · 2027 revisions. Syllabus-linked requirement checklists use the textbook's source-demand review and item-level syllabus matrix. They are concise paraphrases, not official SCSA wording. Source editions · Official course and syllabuses.

Requirements, practice goals and extensions are different. Source-linked checkboxes summarise syllabus demands; chapter goals can include local teaching choices. Extensions have separate labels. A checklist tick or quiz score is a self-check, not teacher verification, full syllabus coverage or a grade prediction.

Offline revision workbookExplained answers

Markdown (.md) downloads are text documents. Print the visible section or use the downloads offline. Expand answers you want printed. Checklist ticks stay in this browser when storage is available; quiz answers stay only in the current page and are lost on refresh. No work is sent to the site.

Topic checklists and retrieval

Tick a point only after an unaided explanation or changed practical attempt. Retain evidence elsewhere and revisit it after a gap. Requirement labels summarise related syllabus demands; the matrix retains the detailed source scope. Some requirements span several chapters.

Cumulative quizzes

Each successive cumulative set adds later units to earlier retrieval. The six sets draw from one bank of 32 questions, so questions repeat across sets and attempts. Use the explanations to diagnose a misconception; repeated scores are not fresh evidence of mastery. These multiple-choice quizzes do not replace written explanations or practical work.

Explained exam-style answers

These 60 original questions are brought together from the existing practice bank. They are formative examples, not official SCSA examination questions or complete papers. Mixed core/extension items are labelled. For a timed, saved written attempt, use Exam practice.

UNIT 1 · Short answer · 2 PRACTICE MARKS

Trace a selection

Syllabus-linked practice: an original question, not an official examination item.

Write the exact output, in order, for this Python program.

score = 7
if score >= 5:
    score = score + 2
else:
    score = score - 1
print(score)
print(score > 10)

Attempt on paper before revealing the guide. Keep the original response and correction separate.

Explained answer, criteria and common mistake
9 False The condition is true, so 2 is added to 7. Nine is not greater than ten.

Why this earns credit

Each criterion is worth one practice mark. Accept equivalent correct wording; check what your original answer actually demonstrates.

  1. First output is 9.
  2. Second output is False (Python Boolean spelling).

Common mistake: Do not execute both branches or print the condition instead of the final comparison.

Revisit the explanation before trying a changed case.

UNIT 1 · Short answer · 2 PRACTICE MARKS

Represent a value

Syllabus-linked practice: an original question, not an official examination item.

Convert decimal 45 to an eight-bit binary value. Show a place-value calculation to support your answer.

Attempt on paper before revealing the guide. Keep the original response and correction separate.

Explained answer, criteria and common mistake
00101101 32 + 8 + 4 + 1 = 45. The 128, 64, 16 and 2 positions are zero.

Why this earns credit

Each criterion is worth one practice mark. Accept equivalent correct wording; check what your original answer actually demonstrates.

  1. Binary result is 00101101.
  2. Working correctly combines place values 32 + 8 + 4 + 1 = 45.

Common mistake: Write all eight bits. Correct equivalent place-value working is acceptable.

Revisit the explanation before trying a changed case.

UNIT 2 · Short answer · 2 PRACTICE MARKS

Validation and verification

Syllabus-linked practice: an original question, not an official examination item.

A club enters member ages from paper forms. Explain the difference between validating an age and verifying the entered age.

Attempt on paper before revealing the guide. Keep the original response and correction separate.

Explained answer, criteria and common mistake
Validation checks an age against rules, such as a permitted numeric range. Verification compares the entered age with the paper form to check it was copied accurately. An incorrect age on the form can still be copied correctly.

Why this earns credit

Each criterion is worth one practice mark. Accept equivalent correct wording; check what your original answer actually demonstrates.

  1. Validation checks whether an age meets stated rules, such as an integer within an allowed range.
  2. Verification checks that the entered age matches the source form; it does not establish that the original age is true.

Common mistake: A valid value is not necessarily the true age. Award equivalent explanations without requiring the model wording.

Revisit the explanation before trying a changed case.

UNIT 2 · Short answer · 2 PRACTICE MARKS

Choose a primary key

Syllabus-linked practice: an original question, not an official examination item.

A Member table has MemberID, GivenName and FamilyName. MemberID is unique and never empty. Explain why MemberID is a better primary key than FamilyName.

Attempt on paper before revealing the guide. Keep the original response and correction separate.

Explained answer, criteria and common mistake
Each MemberID identifies exactly one member. Two members can share a family name, making FamilyName unsuitable as a unique identifier.

Why this earns credit

Each criterion is worth one practice mark. Accept equivalent correct wording; check what your original answer actually demonstrates.

  1. MemberID uniquely identifies each member record.
  2. Family names may repeat, so FamilyName cannot reliably identify one record.

Common mistake: Do not assume names are unique. A primary key also cannot be null.

Revisit the explanation before trying a changed case.

UNIT 2 · Short answer · 2 PRACTICE MARKS

Filter a table

Syllabus-linked practice: an original question, not an official examination item.

Loan(LoanID, MemberID, Returned) stores Returned as 0 for an active loan and 1 for a returned loan. Write SQL to display only LoanID for active loans.

Attempt on paper before revealing the guide. Keep the original response and correction separate.

Explained answer, criteria and common mistake
SELECT LoanID FROM Loan WHERE Returned = 0; SQL keyword case and a missing final semicolon do not affect these marks. Equivalent SQL that returns the requested result is acceptable.

Why this earns credit

Each criterion is worth one practice mark. Accept equivalent correct wording; check what your original answer actually demonstrates.

  1. SELECT LoanID FROM Loan identifies the required field and table.
  2. WHERE Returned = 0 correctly filters active loans.

Common mistake: Returned = 1 selects completed loans. Selecting every field does not meet the requested output.

Revisit the explanation before trying a changed case.

UNIT 2 · Short answer · 2 PRACTICE MARKS

Respond to phishing

Syllabus-linked practice: an original question, not an official examination item.

An unexpected email demands your school password through an unfamiliar link. Identify one warning sign from the scenario and one suitable response.

Attempt on paper before revealing the guide. Keep the original response and correction separate.

Explained answer, criteria and common mistake
The unfamiliar link requesting a password is suspicious. Do not follow it or send credentials; report the message using the school process. Independently contact support through a known address if needed.

Why this earns credit

Each criterion is worth one practice mark. Accept equivalent correct wording; check what your original answer actually demonstrates.

  1. Identifies the unexpected password request, unfamiliar link or pressure to act as a warning sign.
  2. Does not use the link or disclose the password; reports it through the school process or verifies through a known independent channel.

Common mistake: Replying to the suspicious sender is not independent verification. A warning sign is evidence for caution, not proof on its own.

Revisit the explanation before trying a changed case.

UNIT 1 · Short answer · 2 PRACTICE MARKS

Trace a list

Syllabus-linked practice: an original question, not an official examination item.

Write the final values of total and len(values) after this code runs.

values = [4, 1, 3]
total = 0
for value in values:
    total = total + value

Attempt on paper before revealing the guide. Keep the original response and correction separate.

Explained answer, criteria and common mistake
total = 8 len(values) = 3 The loop visits three items and adds each value once.

Why this earns credit

Each criterion is worth one practice mark. Accept equivalent correct wording; check what your original answer actually demonstrates.

  1. Final total is 8.
  2. len(values) is 3.

Common mistake: The length counts items, not their sum. The loop does not alter the list.

Revisit the explanation before trying a changed case.

UNIT 1 · Short answer · 2 PRACTICE MARKS

Test a boundary

Syllabus-linked practice: an original question, not an official examination item.

A program accepts an integer only when 1 <= quantity <= 5. Give one valid boundary input and one invalid input immediately outside a boundary, with the expected acceptance result for each.

Attempt on paper before revealing the guide. Keep the original response and correction separate.

Explained answer, criteria and common mistake
1 → accepted. 0 → rejected. Alternatively, 5 → accepted and 6 → rejected. Either appropriate boundary can be used for each part.

Why this earns credit

Each criterion is worth one practice mark. Accept equivalent correct wording; check what your original answer actually demonstrates.

  1. Gives 1 or 5 and correctly expects acceptance.
  2. Gives 0 or 6 and correctly expects rejection.

Common mistake: A typical valid value such as 3 does not test a boundary. Include the expected result.

Revisit the explanation before trying a changed case.

UNIT 1 · Extended response · 7 PRACTICE MARKS

Design a score summary

Syllabus-linked practice: an original question, not an official examination item.

A Pygame game stores each round score in a one-dimensional list. Scores are whole numbers from 0 to 50. Design an algorithm, using pseudocode or Python, to display the number of rounds, total score and highest score. Handle an empty list explicitly. Explain two useful tests, including inputs and expected results. You do not need to write Pygame drawing code.

Attempt on paper before revealing the guide. Keep the original response and correction separate.

Explained answer, criteria and common mistake
IF length(scores) = 0 THEN DISPLAY "No rounds", 0, 0, "No highest score" ELSE total ← 0 highest ← scores[0] FOR EACH score IN scores total ← total + score IF score > highest THEN highest ← score ENDIF NEXT score DISPLAY length(scores), total, highest ENDIF Test [10, 0, 30]: 3 rounds, total 40, highest 30. Test []: zero rounds and total, no highest score. Correct equivalent algorithms are acceptable, including suitable built-ins because this question does not prohibit them.

Why this earns credit

Each criterion is worth one practice mark. Accept equivalent correct wording; check what your original answer actually demonstrates.

  1. Checks for an empty list before trying to read its first item.
  2. For an empty list, reports zero rounds/total and no highest score (or a clear no-rounds message).
  3. For a non-empty list, correctly obtains the number of rounds.
  4. Correctly accumulates the total across all items.
  5. Correctly finds the maximum, with valid initialisation (for example, the first item).
  6. Gives a non-empty test with correct expected count, total and maximum.
  7. Gives an empty-list test with the expected no-rounds behaviour.

Common mistake: Do not index scores[0] before checking for an empty list. A test needs expected results, not just an input.

Revisit the explanation before trying a changed case.

One member can have many loans, while each loan references one member. Names are stored once in Member, so updating a name does not require editing every loan. Limit editing to authorised club staff using individual accounts and suitable permissions. Make regular separate backups and test restoration so records can be recovered after loss or corruption. Equivalent field choices and suitable explained controls are acceptable.

Equivalent designs and concrete tests meeting these requirements are acceptable.

Why this earns credit

  1. Uses a two-dimensional list/array for tile values accessed by row and column.
  2. Uses a dictionary mapping unique item IDs to descriptions or metadata.
  3. Places shared position/movement behaviour in Actor and uses inheritance for Player and Hazard.
  4. Explains overridden update behaviour for input-driven Player and patrol-driven Hazard.
  5. Describes updating state before drawing that state, with drawing not changing gameplay values.
  6. Gives a movement or wall-boundary test with a specific expected outcome.
  7. Gives an item lookup or patrol test with a specific expected outcome.

UNIT 4 · Extended response · 7 PRACTICE MARKS

Design a reliable booking change

Syllabus-linked practice: an original question, not an official examination item.

A booking service stores Workshop(WorkshopID, Title, Capacity) and Booking(BookingID, WorkshopID, StudentID). A booking must refer to an existing workshop; a student must not book the same workshop twice. Staff can change capacity. Explain suitable database constraints, how the application should safely use user-supplied values in SQL, one suitable staff access control, and a recovery measure. Include an example check for the duplicate-booking rule.

Attempt on paper before revealing the guide. Keep the original response and correction separate.

Explained answer, criteria and common mistake
Use WorkshopID and BookingID as primary keys. Require Booking.WorkshopID and StudentID to be NOT NULL, enforce the WorkshopID foreign key, and add UNIQUE(WorkshopID, StudentID). In SQLite, a nullable foreign key can contain NULL without matching a parent, and UNIQUE permits NULLs, so those constraints alone do not enforce mandatory booking identity. Enable and verify foreign-key enforcement for every SQLite connection before the transaction. Use parameterised SQL, such as placeholders bound to user-supplied values, so those values are treated as data rather than SQL instructions. Test a second booking of the same workshop for the same student: the duplicate must be rejected and the original retained. Restrict capacity updates to authorised staff roles. Keep separate regular backups and test restoration to support recovery. Equivalent constraints, tests and explained controls are acceptable; exact SQL syntax is not required.

Why this earns credit

Each criterion is worth one practice mark. Accept equivalent correct wording; check what your original answer actually demonstrates.

  1. Identifies suitable primary keys for Workshop and Booking.
  2. Requires Booking.WorkshopID to be NOT NULL and a foreign key to an existing Workshop.
  3. Requires StudentID to be NOT NULL and uses a unique constraint on (WorkshopID, StudentID) to prevent duplicate student bookings.
  4. Uses parameterised SQL to pass user-supplied values separately from the SQL statement, rather than concatenating them.
  5. Tests a second booking for the same StudentID and WorkshopID and expects rejection, with the original booking preserved.
  6. Restricts capacity edits to authorised staff with suitable roles/permissions and explains protecting the data.
  7. Proposes separate regular backups with tested restoration and explains recovery after loss/corruption.

Common mistake: A foreign key alone does not stop the same student booking twice or make the reference mandatory. NOT NULL is needed for required identifiers; the composite unique constraint prevents repeated non-NULL pairs. Parameterised SQL helps prevent SQL injection; it does not replace access control or validation.

Revisit the explanation before trying a changed case.

Plan a small classroom network

Connect the 12 computers and a network-capable printer to a suitably sized switch in a star. Connect the switch to the school router for other IP networks. Suitable Ethernet cabling suits fixed workstations and avoids relying on shared radio conditions. Apply individual accounts and appropriate printer permissions. total = 0 above = 0 for row in grid: for reading in row: total = total + reading if reading > 10: above = above + 1 print(total, above) [[10, 11], [0, 15]] → total 36, count 2. [[0, 0], [0, 0]] → total 0, count 0. Equivalent nested algorithms are acceptable.

UNIT 3 · Extended response · 7 PRACTICE MARKS

A game has a player, patrolling hazards and collectible items indexed by unique IDs. Explain shared Actor state, inheritance and specialised update behaviour.   4. Uses a dictionary mapping unique item IDs to item data for lookup.
  5. Drawing reads state without changing score, position or other gameplay state.
  6. Tests two instances and expects changing one position/score not to change the other instance.
  7. Tests a subclass update with a stated input/initial state and a concrete expected movement or patrol result.

Run the related inserts in one transaction. Commit after all required inserts succeed; roll back if any fails so the database does not retain only part of the order.

Distinguish encrypting a message for later recovery from hashing a message to produce a comparison digest.

Attempt on paper before revealing the guide. Keep the original response and correction separate.

Explained answer, criteria and common mistake
Encryption transforms plaintext into ciphertext that can be decrypted with the appropriate key. Hashing produces a digest; comparing digests can help detect changes, but does not recover the message.

Why this earns credit

Each criterion is worth one practice mark. Accept equivalent correct wording; check what your original answer actually demonstrates.

  1. Explains that encryption can be reversed using the appropriate key to recover the message.
  2. Explains that hashing produces a digest for comparison and is not designed to recover the original message.

Common mistake: Hashing is not encryption without a key. A digest alone does not establish who created the message.

Revisit the explanation before trying a changed case.

Attempt on paper before revealing the guide. Keep the original response and correction separate.

Explained answer, criteria and common mistake
Symmetric encryption uses a shared secret key. Asymmetric encryption uses a public/private key pair; a message encrypted with a recipient’s public key is decrypted using the corresponding private key.

Why this earns credit

Each criterion is worth one practice mark. Accept equivalent correct wording; check what your original answer actually demonstrates.

  2. Asymmetric encryption uses a related public/private key pair; in public-key encryption the public key encrypts and the corresponding private key decrypts.

Common mistake: Do not describe the public key as secret. Digital signatures use the pair for a different operation from encrypting a confidential message.

Remove a transitive dependency

Syllabus-linked practice: an original question, not an official examination item.

Asset(AssetID, AssetName, RoomID, RoomName) stores one room per asset. AssetID is the primary key, RoomID determines RoomName, and room names may repeat. Explain the transitive dependency and an update anomaly. Decompose the table into two suitable tables with keys and a relationship. Explain a rule preventing an asset from referencing a non-existent room. Assume all attributes hold atomic values.

Attempt on paper before revealing the guide. Keep the original response and correction separate.

Explained answer, criteria and common mistake
AssetID → RoomID and RoomID → RoomName, so RoomName depends transitively on AssetID. Partial room-name edits can make the same RoomID appear with different names. Decompose into Room(RoomID PK, RoomName) and Asset(AssetID PK, AssetName, RoomID FK). Reference Room.RoomID from Asset.RoomID and enforce the foreign-key constraint. RoomName is stored once per room; a name change no longer requires edits to each asset. RoomName is not a suitable key because names may repeat.

Why this earns credit

Each criterion is worth one practice mark. Accept equivalent correct wording; check what your original answer actually demonstrates.

  1. Identifies AssetID → RoomID → RoomName as the transitive dependency.
  2. Explains an update anomaly: changing a room name in only some asset rows leaves inconsistent names for the same RoomID.
  3. Defines Room(RoomID, RoomName) with RoomID as primary key.
  4. Defines Asset(AssetID, AssetName, RoomID) with AssetID as primary key.
  5. Identifies Asset.RoomID as a foreign key referencing Room.RoomID.
  6. Explains that storing the room name once removes this transitive dependency from Asset and avoids repeated room-name updates.
  7. Requires an enforced foreign-key constraint so a non-null Asset.RoomID must refer to an existing Room row.

Common mistake: Keep the linking RoomID in Asset. Decomposition without the relationship loses which room contains each asset.

Revisit the explanation before trying a changed case.

UNIT 4 · Extended response · 7 PRACTICE MARKS

Protect a school booking service

Syllabus-linked practice: an original question, not an official examination item.

A school booking service faces stolen staff passwords, accidental record deletion and attempts by student accounts to edit capacity. Propose and justify controls for each risk, plus useful audit logging. Describe one permission test and one recovery test with expected outcomes. Explain one remaining limitation after the controls are applied.

Attempt on paper before revealing the guide. Keep the original response and correction separate.

Explained answer, criteria and common mistake
Use suitable MFA for staff sign-in; enforce staff-only capacity-edit permissions at the application/database boundary. Keep separate regular backups for recovery and log who changed a booking or capacity, when, and whether the operation succeeded. Test that a student edit is rejected and capacity remains unchanged. Restore a known backup into a safe test environment and compare recovered records with expected records. Some changes since the last backup may still be lost; controls reduce risk rather than eliminate it. Equivalent justified controls, concrete tests and relevant limitations are acceptable.

Why this earns credit

Each criterion is worth one practice mark. Accept equivalent correct wording; check what your original answer actually demonstrates.

  1. Proposes multi-factor authentication and explains why a stolen password alone should be insufficient to sign in.
  2. Restricts capacity changes to authorised staff and explains least privilege for student accounts.
  3. Uses separate regular backups and explains recovery after accidental deletion.
  4. Logs relevant changes with actor, time and action/result to support investigation.
  5. Tests a student capacity-edit attempt and expects rejection with capacity unchanged.
  6. Tests restoration from a known backup in a safe test environment and expects the selected records to be recovered correctly.
  7. Explains a relevant residual limitation, such as deletion after the latest backup causing some data loss, compromised recovery channels, or logs needing review/protection.

Common mistake: Hiding a button is not an enforced permission check. A backup must be restorable, and logging alone does not prevent an unauthorised change.

Revisit the explanation before trying a changed case.

Keep supporting extensions separate

These can deepen understanding or support a local project. They do not automatically add syllabus requirements. If your teacher includes one in an issued task, use the stated teaching and assessment scope.

SUPPORT BOOKLET + ENRICHMENT CONTEXT

LEFT JOIN extension and support-booklet HAVING

HAVING is shown in the official support booklet (printed p22), after GROUP BY. LEFT JOIN is additional to the explicitly listed INNER JOIN work. Do not label both optional-only or treat support-booklet examples as a separate new unit-content list; teach the relevant technique before assessment.

Open supporting practice

Optional retrieval

Why can COUNT(*) show one for an unmatched left-side row?

Explained support answer

The outer join preserves one row with NULL child fields. COUNT(child_key) instead counts non-NULL matches.

SUPPORT / IMPLEMENTATION / ENRICHMENT CONTEXT

Explicit SQLite transaction control

ACID and the role of database transactions remain syllabus-linked Year 12 requirements. This supporting lab adds explicit BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK syntax in a chosen SQLite tool; those commands are not an extra prescribed keyword list. Teach the chosen tool/driver behaviour before requiring the implementation locally.

Open supporting practice

Optional retrieval

Does an ordinary statement error always undo earlier statements automatically?

Explained support answer

No. Recovery depends on the DBMS/error and transaction boundary. Use an explicit, tested rollback strategy for the logical operation.

A recorder produces 9 MB/s and writes 6 MB/s. How quickly does an initially empty 24 MB buffer fill?

Explained support answer

It grows by 3 MB/s and fills after 24 / 3 = 8 seconds under the stated constant-rate assumptions.
